headline: No RBA rate cuts through 2027; potential hike to 4.85% in February, with core inflation remaining stubbornly above 3%
reasoning: Robertson argues that while August trimmed mean inflation moderated to 0.24% monthly (annualising to ~2.9%), the RBA will remain on hold through end-2026 and is unlikely to cut in 2027. He expects Q3 CPI (due October 28) to come in around 0.9% for the quarter, or 3.5–3.6% year-on-year — still too high. He flags oil back above USD 100/barrel through September-October, record US diesel prices, and Australia's disproportionately high per-capita diesel reliance as key upside inflation risks. He sees a possible rate hike to 4.85% in February and draws a parallel to 2024 when markets prematurely priced in cuts while core inflation remained sticky.
quote: We are a bit of an outlier for next year and that we're not expecting rate cuts next year, whereas the bulk of the market are, albeit in the second half of the year. Uh, so if I think about where, uh, or the drivers of inflation again, great that we had that moderation in August, but that does predate the oil price being back above 100 USD a barrel. Um, which occurred through September or October, and in particular the diesel price and US diesel will hit a record high in the States. A lot of discussion over the last week or two around diesel reserves in the US and Europe. And of course, Australia per capita has a higher reliance on diesel than any other advanced economy in the world. So, um, yes, we are again pleased to see a slight moderation in inflation, but we're somewhat pessimistic about the possibility of core inflation being back below 3% next year. And that's why, as well as potentially seeing a rate hike to 4.85 in February, when not of the view that the RBA are likely to be in a position to cut rates in the back end of 2027.

headline: Australian recession probability only ~15% in next 12 months; demand still resilient but productive capacity insufficient, keeping inflation elevated
reasoning: Robertson says recession is not his base case, estimating only a ~15% probability over the next 12 months, above the historical baseline but not alarming. He notes GDP growth rebounded to 2.5% late last year, but the economy lacked the productive capacity to meet that demand, reigniting inflation even before the Middle East conflict. Consumer and business confidence are both depressed, with business conditions in negative territory, but business investment (especially tech CapEx) provides an offsetting support. He flags that the global tech investment trend carries its own inflationary risks.
quote: I'd say right now that a probability of a recession in the next 12 months is only about 15%. I don't expect it to happen, but 15% a little higher than obviously, if you look at the long term trend where we've had a recession in 91. Didn't have another one until the pandemic, and let's hope it's sometime before the next. Um, I think the counter to the dangers around recessionary risks is there's actually still a reasonable amount of demand in the economy. And this is the thing we saw with the rebound in GDP growth towards the end of last year. GDP growth, um, rose to 2.5%. Unfortunately, our economy didn't have the productive capacity to meet that demand, which is why inflation is back. Even was back prior to the Middle East conflict. Uh, but I'll just maybe round out the answer to that question by saying, at least fortunately, we're seeing this uplift in business investment CapEx all looks fairly promising at the moment. A lot of that's around tech investment, but this is a global trend. Um, and again, it's a global environment where unfortunately there are inflationary risks that come with that.
